title: QRÖMELIFE
excerpt: Quavo has released *QRÖMELIFE*, his third solo album, a 14-track record executive produced by Pharrell Williams and developed with him over more than a year and a half.
body:
Quavo has released *QRÖMELIFE*, his third solo album, a 14-track record executive produced by Pharrell Williams and developed with him over more than a year and a half. It follows 2023's *Rocket Power*, an album made much closer to Takeoff's death and shaped directly by grief. *QRÖMELIFE* comes from a later point in that story. Loss is still present, but Quavo is no longer writing as if it is the only subject available to him. The album has more room for pleasure, family, ambition and the ordinary routines that continue even after a life has been permanently changed.

Pharrell became the central collaborator during sessions that stretched from Louis Vuitton's headquarters in Paris to a yacht in Miami. Quavo has said the challenge was not to replace his established sound but to recover parts of it that had become less visible, especially the melodic flexibility that let him move between Migos records, solo singles and features without sounding locked into one mode. "Trance (Walk It Down)" is a good example. Heavy low end and quick percussion push it toward the club, while Quavo spends most of the track bending phrases rather than attacking them. The loose, tuneful delivery is exactly the side of Quavo that Pharrell encouraged him to revisit, and it gives the song a very different temperature from the heavier mood of *Rocket Power*.

The title comes from Quavo's own use of the word "qrome," which he connects to "chromosome." He describes a qrome state as the condition of carrying something difficult with you while still getting up and handling everyday life. His example is intentionally mundane. Someone can go through a loss or crisis and still have to show up for a nine-to-five the next morning. That explanation gives the record a clearer center than the chrome imagery around its rollout might suggest. *QRÖMELIFE* is less interested in pretending hardship produces a clean transformation than in the fact that it simply becomes part of the person who survives it.

[apple:album:6817200688]

One of the album's most significant moments arrives on "Away," which brings Offset back onto a Quavo record after the public split that preceded Takeoff's death. The reunion comes after years in which both men had to work through the same loss separately and eventually repaired their relationship. They are also sorting through ideas for another Migos project, though Quavo has been careful about what continuing the group would mean without its third member. He has said the chemistry with Offset is still there, but any future Migos release would have to honor Takeoff rather than simply use the name because the two surviving members can.

That restraint matters because *QRÖMELIFE* is not built as a Migos nostalgia exercise. Even when the album leans back into familiar Atlanta rhythms, Quavo sounds more interested in how his voice can move through a song than in recreating a specific era of the group. Pharrell's influence is most useful when it leaves room for that instinct. The record can pivot from harder drums to brighter, more melodic passages without turning every change in production into a showcase. It is a more relaxed album than *Rocket Power*, not because the years between them have erased anything, but because Quavo no longer has to make every song carry the full weight of what happened.

Fatherhood gives the album its most concrete change in perspective. Quavo recently revealed that he has become a father to a daughter and has spoken about how seriously he takes the role because his own father died when he was four. He wants to be present for the parts of his child's life that he never had a father there to see. The short film released with *QRÖMELIFE* moves through old Migos footage, Takeoff, studio sessions and the years that followed before ending with Quavo holding his daughter. For an album built around what a person carries with them, that final image says more than another explanation of the title could.
